articles.title: What happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment? | Simar Bajaj and Joseph Sakran
articles.text:
In healthcare, there’s growing concern over doctors becoming less clinically adept as they increasingly rely on AI tools. But what about the trainees – medical students, residents and fellows – who are using these tools before they have built their own clinical judgment? The idea of deskilling implies that someone possessed an ability and then lost it. Here, the danger is not just deskilling but never-skilling. Although a doctor who has forgotten how to reason is recoverable, one who never learned how may not be.

OpenEvidence, essentially an AI chatbot for clinicians, has given this concern its most concrete form. About two-thirds of US doctors actively use OpenEvidence, asking about puzzling symptoms, drug interactions and clinical guidelines, getting responses within seconds, anchored in the latest research. Trainees, unsurprisingly, have also begun to use this AI tool in many of the same ways – but at a far more formative stage.

For example, trainees once asked to build a list of potential diagnoses might struggle and offer an incomplete set, learning what they missed, sometimes painfully. Now, trainees can simply ask OpenEvidence and get a nearly perfect answer, complete with possibilities they might have never considered and none of the embarrassment of having overlooked them. Repeating this answer on the wards may make the trainee look prepared and even impress the supervising doctor.

However, this performance can also conceal the very deficit that training is meant to reveal: that the struggle is the point. Medical training, more than most professions, is an apprenticeship. A student becomes a resident, a resident becomes a fellow, and a fellow becomes an attending – every step shaped by failure, uncertainty and increasing responsibility. With years of repetition and watchful supervision, the habits of clinical reasoning slowly become part of the physician’s inner architecture.

Technology has long shifted how people learn medicine, from advanced imaging to electronic medical records. But AI is different, not just expanding what doctors can see but inserting itself into the cognitive machinery that training is meant to build. As these tools become more capable and the physician’s role increasingly involves supervising them, experienced clinicians may have enough intuition and independent judgment to critically evaluate the machine’s answers. But for trainees whose understanding of medicine is being formed alongside AI, the relationship is more fraught. Can they really question the reasoning that shaped their own? What happens when the generation trained by AI becomes the generation responsible for catching its mistakes? With unchecked use among trainees, we risk creating supervisors of reasoning before we create reasoners.

The stakes of that question are growing: a recent study in Nature Medicine found that tools pulling from the latest medical literature, like OpenEvidence does, can be less reliable than they appear and, in some cases, less accurate than general-purpose AI chatbots. The problem of misplaced trust is already embedded in the AI that trainees are using today.

To be clear, many trainees sense the trap, telling us they know that tools such as OpenEvidence can become a crutch. But these trainees also feel stuck in an arms race: if everyone else is using AI to sound more prepared, opting out feels like unilateral disarmament. The solution, then, cannot rest on individual restraint. It has to be structural.

That is why medical schools and residency programs need to shape not just whether trainees use AI, but when. No one can police every search on every phone, nor should they. But supervising doctors can build a simple expectation – reason first, consult AI second – and assess accordingly. Trainees should have to make their unaided first pass visible, committing to a leading diagnosis, naming the dangerous possibilities to rule out, and explaining what to do next. In practice, that might mean a resident who admits a patient overnight first writes a brief “pre-AI assessment” after the history and physical exam. On rounds, when a new lab result or symptom changes the case, the attending might need to pause the team – before anyone can consult AI – to ask how this changes the diagnosis or treatment plan.

As AI becomes more deeply integrated into medicine, this will feel cumbersome and inefficient. But such friction is purposeful: the learning scientists Elizabeth and Robert Bjork describe how “desirable difficulties” slow performance in the moment but improve retention and transfer of skills over time. In fact, used after an independent attempt, AI could actually serve as a powerful tutor, showing trainees what they missed and what they overemphasized.

Sequencing, however, may not be enough on its own. Aviation thus offers a useful precedent: pilots in training are not taught to avoid autopilot but to preserve their manual competence. The Federal Aviation Administration even advises pilots to maintain manual flying skills by periodically disengaging automation and hand-flying. Medicine needs similar discipline, with trainees required to periodically work through no-AI cases and assessed on their unaided reasoning to reveal potential drift.

Finally, trainees should be taught to interrogate AI itself. Programs could run the medical equivalent of flight simulator drills, built from real clinical cases: for example, a polished AI-generated assessment with a subtle flaw. Afterward, attendings could debrief not only whether the trainee reached the right answer but also when they trusted the tool, when they questioned it, and when they found the flaw. Just as important, attendings should mix in AI outputs that are perfectly accurate, so students learn not reflexive skepticism but disciplined judgment.

None of this is an argument for making medical training harder for its own sake or romanticizing humiliation as pedagogy. In every generation of medicine, there is a temptation to confuse difficulty with virtue, but the struggle to independently reason through a patient’s case is not hazing but a core competency.

AI is here to stay, and patients stand to benefit from its speed and reach. But patients will also need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason – doctors whose reasoning is not subordinated to it. Although AI can reason over the facts it is given, a trainee who has seen pneumonia that looks like pneumonia, then pneumonia that looks like heart failure, then heart failure that looks like pneumonia, develops a richer bedside judgment: what to notice, what to question, and when a familiar pattern should be distrusted. That is what medical training is trying to produce. AI should help augment this, not replace it.

articles.title: Disney agrees deal to let TikTokers use its characters in videos
articles.text:
Disney and TikTok have agreed a deal which will allow creators to use clips from Disney films, including its subsidiaries, in their videos.

It means clips from hit franchises like Star Wars, Toy Story and the Marvel Cinematic Universe will soon start popping up in videos - which will also be shared on Disney's short-form video platform, Verts.

The scheme will be launched in the US before being rolled out to other countries.

Neither company shared financial details of the agreement, although it follows the collapse of a $1bn (£745m) deal between Disney and OpenAI which would have let people use its characters in AI-generated videos.

That agreement was cancelled in March when OpenAI shut down its AI video generation tool Sora, citing a decision to focus on other parts of its business.

"Today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways," said Disney's chief marketing and brand officer Asad Ayaz, following the TikTok deal being announced.

"Disney owns some of the world's biggest franchises but ownership of attention is shifting towards creators," social media expert Matt Navarra told BBC News.

"Hollywood used to market at fans - now it needs to give fans the raw materials to market with it, and that is quite a profound shift."

TikTok said its platform saw an average of 6.5 million posts relating to film and TV per day last year.

Fans like to use clips from films and TV shows in their videos, but without express permission, they would often be taken down due to copyright claims.

This makes it harder for a wide audience to engage with fan-created content around a big release.

TikTok would also benefit from the "credibility of becoming a formal distribution partner to one of Hollywood's biggest studios," Navarra said.

He added that TikTok's recommendation algorithm gives it the power to "influence which character or scene or forgotten franchise suddenly becomes very valuable again".

Disney and TikTok said a jointly-run programme would boost some creators' videos and give them access to exclusive events.

"This is a deal that repositions and recovers Disney in the UGC [user-generated content] space following the content gap left by the sudden collapse of Sora," Gareth Sutcliffe from Enders Analysis said.

But he said it was not without risk.

"There is an ongoing safety debate around TikTok under European online rules," he said.

"At a minimum, Disney will need to employ significant guardrails to curate the creator content that is selected."

Online creators and influencers are becoming more important to brands' marketing strategies.

Last year, a report from Oxford Economics said YouTube content creators contributed £2.2bn to the UK economy in 2024 and supported 45,000 jobs.

There is also a recognition that even very small influencers, who focus on niche topics, might have lower follower counts but come with a hyper-engaged audience.

Disney launched its short form video platform Verts in the US in March, with plans to expand that further around the world.

articles.title: Radio Caroline breached Ofcom rules after mistakenly announcing King Charles's death
articles.text:
Radio Caroline has been found in breach of broadcasting rules after it mistakenly announced the death of King Charles III.

The station aired three pre-recorded announcements falsely stating the King had died during the Barry Marsh Show on 19 May.

The messages claimed the "news media" had "confirmed" the death, and were followed by the national anthem and 16 minutes of silence on DAB+, while AM listeners heard back-up music. A correction and apology was broadcast 30 minutes later.

The ruling by media watchdog Ofcom stated that once the staff member who accidentally played the files realised what they had done, they stopped playing them, "panicked and left the premises".

Ofcom said the incident breached Rule 5.1, which requires news to be reported with due accuracy, and Rule 5.2, which says significant mistakes must be corrected quickly.

It described the false announcement as a "very significant inaccuracy" on a matter of "very high public interest".

The mistake happened after a staff member carrying out maintenance accessed pre‑recorded obituary files intended for use in the event of the King's death.

Ofcom said the files were played "out of curiosity", cutting off the presenter's remote stream and putting the announcements on air.

Radio Caroline said the presenter did not realise they were off air because, as is common practice, they were streaming the programme remotely.

The station said its presenter "would not realise that they had gone 'off air' unless they were monitoring their output via an internet monitor."

It added that the station director was across the station's AM output but was on a call when the inaccurate announcement was broadcast.

The station director noticed the issue only when he heard continuous music instead of the scheduled programme and contacted the engineer, who was aware of the issue and was already investigating.

A brief apology was then made, with the presenter saying the earlier information had been "incorrect" and that it was due to "a technical issue."

The station said it "took the matter very seriously" and acted "as soon as possible".

The staff member involved has been reprimanded, and the obituary files have been moved off the studio desktop to prevent a repeat incident.

Radio Caroline noted Ofcom received only two complaints about the incident and said the station is "100% volunteer-led" without the resources of larger broadcasters.

Founded in 1964 as an offshore pirate station, Radio Caroline broadcast from a ship until 1991, when it was shipwrecked off the Kent coast.

The station is still based off the north-east Essex coast, although many presenters broadcast their shows remotely.

articles.title: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
articles.text:
The first Game of Thrones stage spin-off has been launched by the Royal Shakespeare Company, and the verdict from most theatre critics is that it's a worthy addition to the epic fantasy franchise.

Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a prequel set shortly before the events of George RR Martin's first book and the all-conquering TV series, officially opened at the RSC in Stratford-upon-Avon this weekend.

The Telegraph awarded four stars to the "spellbinding spectacle", while the Guardian's four-star review said it features "spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance".

The Times was more lukewarm, giving three stars and saying the play "lacks pace, sex and gore".

The Game of Thrones origin story is epic in both ambition and execution – it has taken seven years to reach the stage, clocks in at three hours 45 minutes, and features a 36-strong cast.

The characters include younger versions of familiar figures like Ned Stark, Jaime Lannister and Robert Baratheon; and others whose fates were key to the events in the main saga, such as Lyanna Stark, Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and the "mad king" himself, Aerys II Targaryen.

After opening in Shakespeare's home town, the RSC will hope it can go on to replicate the success of other spin-off plays like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Stranger Things: The First Shadow, which have both had lengthy runs in the West End and on Broadway.

The Shakespeare connection stems from the fact Martin's novels were heavily inspired by Shakespeare's history plays, especially those about the battles between the houses of Lancaster and York during the Wars of the Roses in the 15th Century.

Game of Thrones' US creator was heavily involved in the play, stationing a representative in rehearsals at all times, and he attended the opening night in Stratford on Saturday.

In the Guardian's review, Mark Lawson wrote, external: "Purists will object that, rather than staging Shakespeare-adjacent populist spin-offs, the RSC should be offering its house dramatist's royal dramas plain.

"The counter argument is that hitching on to a cultural juggernaut may bring in new sources of income and audiences."

Audiences will respond differently to the play depending on whether they are already loyal Game of Thrones fans, and Lawson's four-star rating attempted to bridge that gap.

"This feels like a five-star production for most devoted throners but a three-star for those who haven't seen the TV series," he said.

Metro's critic Dave Freak agreed, external, also bestowing four stars.

"As a stand-alone piece of theatre, The Mad King scrapes through," he wrote. "But as an extension of the Game of Thrones world, it scores well, shifting the narrative to the stage with suitably theatrical thrust."

The Telegraph's Dominic Cavendish wrote, external: "At almost four hours, it's a long evening, sometimes too dense with detail, and it lacks the grit and gore (not to mention the nudity) of the TV series.

"Still, it capably serves newbies and devotees, and speaks in a timely fashion to our age of unruly leaders."

He added: "It's not up there, yet, with the Harry Potter or Stranger Things prequels but, on balance, the Game of Thrones franchise has yet another worthwhile and lucrative spin-off on its hands."

The Times' critic Clive Davis, external had greater reservations, writing that while the play "gives hardcore GoT fans a chance to go hunting for 'Easter eggs', it seldom comes close to matching the grim aura of the TV series".

He wrote: "Duncan Macmillan's script is sorely lacking in poetry. Events plod forward, one after the other, and although Michael Shaeffer is a thoroughly compelling presence as the cruel and chronically unstable monarch Aerys, other performances seem nuance-free. Too many lines are simply shouted. You expect better of the RSC."

Davis concluded: "It goes without saying that there are more than enough GoT devotees to keep the box office ticking over for the rest of eternity, but only the most dedicated of them will have the energy for this marathon."

Others were more enthusiastic, and Whatsonstage's Sarah Crompton's five-star review, external said the play is "a triumph; a soaring, surging spectacle and a latter-day history play, both serious and popular".

She added: "It is a remarkable achievement, wonderfully directed by [Dominic] Cooke and superbly acted by every member of the 35-strong ensemble. The result is a brilliant exhibition of how theatre can create magic."

The Independent's Alice Saville, external, awarding four stars, said the "stellar stage show has all the thrillingly staged battles, gory deaths and, yes, dragons that the most bloodthirsty fan could hope for".

"But there's also a surprising amount of heart – of the warm, still-beating kind – as it lingers on the faces of its fallen," she said.

Cooke said there were "lots of similarities" with Shakespeare, especially the themes of "dynastic struggle, what it means to have power, intergenerational conflict and powerful families".

Martin has been "very supportive" in the process of creating the play, the director added.

"He's been collaborative in terms of the development of the script. We've worked very closely with him. And George, I think, picked up quite quickly that we were very serious about honouring what he'd done."

Tamara Harvey, the RSC's co-artistic director, said: "George himself talks about how Shakespeare and the Wars of the Roses inspired him to write these stories.

"So the connections feel very deep, and of course themes are shared: power, love, succession, battles for who gets to rule who – it's all there in the Shakespeare history, just as it is in Game of Thrones."

Asked about future plans for the play, Harvey replied: "We're hoping as many people as possible get to see it, and that starts here in Stratford. And from then, who knows?"

articles.title: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor cancels live event after plagiarism row
articles.text:
Jason Arday has cancelled an appearance in London next month, following his resignation as a Cambridge professor in the wake of allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

Arday's talk at the Royal Geographical Society's conference has been "cancelled at the request of the speaker", the organisation said.

He is also no longer listed on the websites of two other scheduled events in the coming months.

Arday - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his early work, but said he was not a "liar" and that the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

He had been due to take part in a "fireside chat" at the Royal Geographical Society's conference in London on 2 September.

Arday's appearance at Topping & Company book shop in Edinburgh on 18 September is no longer listed on the website and has reportedly also been cancelled. The shop declined to comment.

He was also announced as a guest for the Arizona Women's Board Authors' Luncheon on 24 October, but is no longer listed on the event's website.

He is still listed as a speaker for the Stroud Book Festival in Gloucestershire in November.

In another development, BBC News has learned that Arday resigned on Sunday as a publication director and trustee of the British Sociological Association (BSA), the national body for sociology academics.

The BSA, to which Arday gave a lecture earlier this year claiming black academics were being targeted in "evil" ways, told the BBC it would shortly amend its website to reflect the change.

It was one of multiple roles Arday held in various organisations.

The NHS Race and Health Observatory - which studies racial and ethnic inequality in health - lists him as a member of its "academic reference advisory group", citing his now-out-of-date Cambridge title. Arday was also named as a fellow of the Royal Society of Arts by Cambridge when it appointed him.

Neither organisation replied to the BBC's request for clarification on whether they remained current roles.

Arday also sat on ITV's Cultural Advisory Council and as an expert the Welsh Government's anti-racism external accountability group, but both roles ended earlier this year.

When asked by the BBC, Advance HE declined to confirm whether Arday remains a senior fellow of its formerly named Higher Education Academy, citing data protection law. The senior fellowship is awarded to individuals who "lead or influence the learning and teaching practices of others".

The Runnymede Trust think tank, for whom Arday was a trustee until 2024, released a statement defending him last week and condemning "racialised, hyper-aggressive media scrutiny".

The publisher of Arday's memoir Great and Unfortunate Things is going ahead with its release in the US on Tuesday and in the UK on 27 August as planned.

The book tells the story of his life from being non-verbal until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18, then going through a series of "improbable triumphs and heartbreaking setbacks", before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge.

However, he has been accused of plagiarism in his PhD thesis, and questions have been raised about the reliability of parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5m for charity.

On Wednesday, the University of Cambridge said it had launched an investigation "following new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

Announcing his resignation on the same day, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

articles.title: Tabby Stoecker: Olympic gold medallist joins Strictly Come Dancing 2026 line-up
articles.text:
Olympic gold medallist Tabby Stoecker is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.

The Team GB skeleton racer won gold at the 2026 Winter Olympic Games, and is also a World Cup race winner, a double World Championship medallist and a European Championship medallist.

In a statement, Stoecker said she was "over the moon" to be joining the cast of Strictly 2026.

"I've had the wildest year of my life so far," she continued, "so to be rounding it off with a childhood dream of dancing in the Strictly ballroom is surreal and I can't wait to get stuck in!"

Stoeker is the 13th celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer, Will Best, Jaime Winstone and Dame Sarah Storey.

The final two contestants are set to be announced soon. Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:

Emmerdale actor Lawrence Robb has played Mackenzie 'Mack' Boyd in the ITV soap since 2020.

His other credits include appearing opposite Billie Piper in I Hate Suzie and in stage productions such as Legally Blonde The Musical.

In a statement, the actor joked: "I don't know who's more excited about this, me or my mother.

"I can't quite believe that I am going to be getting my dancing shoes on this September on one of my favourite shows of all time."

He added: "It's a dream come true, and I can't wait to bring my all to ballroom. Wish me luck, and any advice is very welcome - trust me I'll need it!"

Known as the Dogfather, Graeme Hall has appeared on Channel 5's Dog's Behaving (Very) Badly since the show's launch in 2017.

The presenter and dog trainer has also fronted The Dog Hospital and contributed to BBC radio programmes, ITV's This Morning, and wrote a regular column for the Times.

"I can't believe I am joining the cast of Strictly for 2026," Hall said. "I have always loved dancing, so to have the opportunity to learn from the best in the business is a dream come true.

"I have watched the show for years, so to be a part of it feels like a very exciting challenge, albeit more than a bit nerve-wracking! I can't wait to get started. Bring it on!"

Hall has also written books including The Ultimate Kid's Guide to Dogs and previously made a cameo appearance in the hit drama All Creatures Great and Small.

Other celebrities to be confirmed for Strictly this year include former England and Manchester City winger Shaun Wright-Phillips.

The football pundit, who is the son of Arsenal legend Ian Wright, had 36 caps for England and also played for clubs including Chelsea and Queens Park Rangers.

His fancy footwork may have dazzled on the pitch but Wright-Phillips said this latest challenge "is definitely outside my comfort zone".

"Dancing is in my blood - but mainly at family events!" he said. "I'm super excited to get started and really looking forward to the challenge!"

While ex-footballers have had mixed fortunes on previous Strictly series, former soccer star Karen Carney flipped the script last year by winning the coveted glitterball.

Antonia has portrayed dragon-rider Lady Baela Targaryen in HBO's Game of Thrones prequel since 2022. She is currently starring as Eurydice in the Tony Award-winning musical Hadestown in London's West End.

Her acting career began when she was 14 when she appeared in a short film adaptation of The Tempest, before being cast as a guest role in the BBC's Doctors.

The singer and actress has also appeared in series including Nolly, Stay Close, Stath Lets Flats, and Doctor Who.

Antonia said: "I can't quite believe that I will be heading to the Strictly ballroom this September! I have grown up watching Strictly, and I am so excited to take the challenge on and (hopefully!) learn a new skill. See you on the dancefloor!"

Jaime Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.

The actress, who also won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition.

The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me".

"I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"

Winstone has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.

After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year.

Known as Great Britain's most successful Paralympian of all time, Dame Sarah Storey has secured 19 gold medals across the nine Paralympic Games she competed in.

The swimmer and cyclist said embarking on the challenge is "hugely exciting" and she "can't wait to get started".

"I have always loved watching Strictly and my daughter Louisa is a very talented dancer, so to be able to learn from the best and hopefully understand even more about her world, is incredibly motivating!" she said.

The former athlete won four golds at London 2012. She started her career as a swimmer and later switched to cycling, winning 30 Paralympic medals in total.

Best is known for hosting Big Brother with AJ Odudu on ITV since 2023, and as host of the Hits Radio Breakfast Show alongside Fleur East and James Barr.

He said it was "an absolute dream" to be taking to the BBC One contest's dance floor in September, "albeit a pretty terrifying one".

Best added: "I've been lucky to do lots of live telly before, but absolutely nothing like this. And I cannot wait!

"I have no idea if I can actually dance, but bring on the sequins, bring on the quicksteps, bring on the dance floor! I'm going to try to enjoy every minute of it."

Mercer was part of the winning couple on ITV dating show Love Island last year, and also works as a model and DJ, and is an ambassador for a young people's mental health charity.

"I have grown up watching the show with my family and am so excited to now be part of the cast," he said.

Mercer also showcases his Afrobeat, hip-hop and street dance moves on his social media accounts.

"Dancing is a huge passion of mine and I can't wait to learn ballroom and do the foxtrot for the first time!" he added.

Delta Goodrem is also part of this year's celebrity list, with the Australian singer and actress becoming the third celebrity to be announced for the upcoming series.

"I've been incredibly honoured to perform on many different stages throughout my career - from TV, theatre, film sets, to touring my own shows around the world," Goodrem said.

"There is, however, one stage I've never stepped onto and that is the ballroom floor. I'm absolutely thrilled to be joining Strictly and can't wait to get started."

She rose to fame in hit Australian soap opera Neighbours and recently represented her nation in the 2026 edition of the Eurovision Song Contest.

Lacey Turner was the first contestant to be announced for this year's series, which is expected to begin in September.

She said she was "so excited to be making my way to the dance floor", adding that she was a "huge fan" of the show.

Turner, 38, is best known for her role as Stacey Slater on the BBC One soap, which she joined in 2004.

She has won a British Soap Award and National Television Award for her role, and has also starred in TV dramas including the BBC's Our Girl.

In a video posted on Instagram, Turner said she was "so excited and so terrified at the same time" to be taking part in the show.

"But I've had so many friends do Strictly, and I thought it was about time that I pluck up the courage and made my way on to the dance floor."

Dani Dyer, the media personality and daughter of actor Danny Dyer appeared in the launch episode last year, but was then injured in training and pulled out before the competition began.

That incident has not put her off trying again. "I am so excited to be back in the ballroom this September," she said.

"I just cannot wait to get my dancing shoes back on and hopefully this time around I can actually make it to week one! I'm just over the moon and cannot wait to find out who else is doing it."

The 29-year-old, who first found fame on Love Island in 2018, fractured her ankle when she "landed funny" in rehearsals with dance partner Nikita Kuzmin before the competitive episodes began last September.

She was replaced by actress Amber Davies, another former Love Island winner, who went on to reach the Strictly final.

Earlier this year, Dyer was joint winner of Channel 4's Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins, and appeared with her dad in TV show The Dyers' Caravan Park.

Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe will take over as Strictly presenters this year, following the departures of Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.

Ballas, Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke will all return as judges.

Regular pro dancers including Amy Dowden, Dianne Buswell, Katya Jones, Vito Coppola and Aljaz Skorjanec will all be back on the dance floor.

However, professional dancers Gorka Marquez, Nadiya Bychkova, Luba Mushtuk, Karen Hauer and Michelle Tsiakkas will not be returning this year.

articles.title: Fire at Sheffield's Full Monty club thought to be arson
articles.text:
A fire at a working men's club in Sheffield which famously appeared in the 1997 film The Full Monty is believed to have been started deliberately.

The blaze broke out at Shiregreen Working Men's Club on Shiregreen Lane just before 16:45 BST on Sunday, according to South Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service.

A spokesperson said eight fire engines and a turntable ladder were sent to the scene, with no reports of any injuries. Crews left just after midnight and were due to return later to ensure there were no hotspots remaining.

The building has been closed since 2019 and has become derelict in recent years, with a fire also started there deliberately last year.

A fire service spokesperson said the latest blaze was also believed to have been started deliberately.

In 2020, Sheffield City Council refused an application to bulldoze the building after more than 1,000 people signed a petition to save it.

Ann Bentley, who was behind the petition having worked at the club for 15 years, said she was "absolutely devastated" to learn there had been another fire there.

"It meant so much to me," she said of her time working at the club, where she met her husband Roy.

"Every time I pass it I want to cry. I would have loved to have seen it back on its feet."

articles.title: Kamal on making music for 'real ones' and Dave collaboration
articles.text:
He's been backed by British rappers Dave and Central Cee, but rising singer-songwriter Kamal says he'll always focus on making music for the "real ones".

The 24-year-old musician from north-west London has just released his debut album after years of navigating the music industry, having signed to independent label Neighbourhood Recordings as a teenager.

Along the way, his 2020 breakout single Homebody became a lockdown hit and the R&B-tinged track Blue gained him further recognition, including reportedly from US superstar Billie Eilish.

"Apparently she [Billie] put me on a playlist that she'd curated for Spotify, so I mean I was gassed to be part of that sort of taste profile," Kamal tells BBC Newsbeat from his home garden studio in London.

He aims for "honesty" within his music, which also means admitting it was "scary" to ask Brit-award winner Dave to feature on his new album.

"Dave is such a humble guy and he doesn't feel too inaccessible because I feel like he really leads from a love of music, first and foremost," says Kamal.

"Which is the exact same way that I feel."

Dave featuring on his album is a full circle moment as Kamal previously featured on the rapper's 2021 track Mercury.

"I feel like the connection was already established for the most part," Kamal says of their relationship.

"But yeah, it still feels scary when you hit him up because you're like, obviously it is Dave, I grew up listening to him so it feels like a massive moment."

Rapper Dave, who has numerous Brit Awards, Ivor Novellos and a Mercury Prize to his name, opens up Kamal's track, The People That Saved Me, with poignant lyrics about love and memories.

Kamal says the verse was "perfect for the album" and "the kind of message" he wanted to send.

He has also featured on Mobo award-winning rapper Central Cee's 2025 track Now We're Strangers, and joined him on stage at London's The O2 to perform it.

"I feel like the O2 is a dream venue for so many of us musicians so to be up there was proper surreal," he says of that moment.

Amidst the major collaborations, Kamal wants to create music that is meaningful - something which comes across in his work.

"The music is always going to be the leading factor and you don't even get the co-signs unless there's a little something there in the first place," Kamal says.

And he plans to keep his day one fans at the forefront of it all.

"For the people that really love my music, they see the common thread, separately of those external things, of really vulnerable writing, which is what I always try and lead with," he explains.

"I always say I try and lead with honesty in the music, and I feel like that's the best way I can express myself.

"The people that latch onto that are always the real ones at the core of the fan base."

The singer's 13-track album also includes songs like Suffer, which explores topics around love and heartbreak, and All My Favourite People Are Sad, which talks of depression and friendship.

It's a lot of reflection for someone so young, and includes experimental tones which add a different layer to his usual soft singing voice.

Kamal describes his background as a mix of Trinidad, Belize, English and Palestinian and his childhood was filled with music.

But his relationship with music came before any hopes he might have had about making it big - and he says he still has much to learn.

"I feel like there's still a long way to go when I look at my music career, but I'm also very grateful for everything that's happened so far," he says.

And when it comes to the "doomscrolling" generation, Kamal has thoughts.

While he accepts that platforms like TikTok help artists who might not have a "fighting chance in the industry", he says the constant stream of content can sometimes feel like "fast food" music.

"I feel like lots of art forms are a bit more oversaturated now and they feel like they're more content pieces rather than pieces of art," he says.

He feels you have to "weed through" this to try and "maintain some sort of sense of taste".

As he's still in the early stages of his career, Kamal is taking it "day-by-day".

"I'm more just trying to figure out what's the best vibe of music and what's the best sonic and lyric that I can lead with next," he says.

"So I really take it day-by-day, studio session by studio session.

"It feels great, but there's a long way to go still."

articles.title: Andrea Bocelli to play in Wales for first time in 22 years at Land of Song Festival
articles.text:
Andrea Bocelli is set to return to Wales for the first time in 22 years as part of a new festival.

The Italian tenor will take to the Principality Stadium, in Cardiff, for the inaugural Land of Song Festival.

It has been billed as a celebration of the musical heritage of Wales featuring world-renowned artists and choirs, and was inspired by Wales's reputation as the land of song.

The 67-year-old said he was "thrilled" to be making his first ever headline appearance in Wales on such an "unforgettable evening".

Bocelli, who has been blind since the age of 12, is one of the most successful classical artists of all time and has won multiple major awards, six Grammy nominations and a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame during his almost four-decade career.

The classical musician has performed for the royal family, popes and many US presidents, and is famed for hits such as Time To Say Goodbye and The Prayer.

He has also performed at major events around the world, such as the Olympic Games and the World Cup.

Bocelli performed for Leicester fans at the King Power Stadium when the team won the Premier League title in 2016.

He said he called Leicester manager and fellow countryman Claudio Ranieri, and offered to sing in the "big fiesta".

He said he was excited to add Cardiff to the "many extraordinary places around the world" that he had performed in.

He last came to Wales in 2005 as part of Bryn Terfel's Faenol Festival alongside Van Morrison, Alison Moyet and Katherine Jenkins.

Bocelli added: "The country's rich choral heritage and deep connection with music make this city a fitting setting for this special concert."

articles.title: Harry Potter fans force power link diversion to avoid Dobby's grave
articles.text:
Harry Potter fans succeeded in diverting a multimillion-pound power link between the UK and Ireland after they complained it would disturb a "memorial" to Dobby the House Elf.

The £430m Greenlink interconnector links the National Grid to Ireland via 125-mile cable between County Wexford and Freshwater West, a beach in Pembrokeshire where the death of fictional character Dobby was filmed in the Potter films.

Project manager Simon Ludlam told the Energy Revolution podcast the cable was originally "going to go straight through" the tribute, before fans left his firm "hundreds of calls".

"Actually we went quite close to some real Bronze Age remains, but we avoided Dobby's grave," he said.

Ludlam, founder of Etchea Energy, said a BBC News interview about the project had turned into a public relations nightmare after fans got wind of what was to happen.

He told the podcast that during the filmed interview he had pointed out where the cable would go underground, saying: "We did the shot, we finished I went back to London, and they then aired it a couple of weeks later.

"And we got hundreds of calls, I mean hundreds of calls."

A colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently, we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said, 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said, 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

articles.title: Zainab Jiwa: My viral moment with Zendaya at The Odyssey premiere
articles.text:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”

Arriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.

She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.

Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.

Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview the stars.

"I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”

Today, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers such as Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal, Tom Hiddleston and Zendaya herself – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.

She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.

It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).

She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.

Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs.

"I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.

For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.

She admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too.

"I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'"

"I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."

But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different.

"Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".

She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.

Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".

With 660,000 followers on TikTok and close to 400,000 on Instagram, she's becoming a key content creator in this field. But she also faces criticism - including from some who claim her outfits are not modest enough.

"There's always hate in this industry," she says.

But she adds: "For every negative comment, there's so many positive ones.

"If I'm doing it to inspire other people, or entertain other people, or educate other people, if that's still happening, then I really don't care about the rest."

For now though, Zainab is swept up in enjoying a string of blockbusters.

"The summer's felt good for film - I think it's exciting," she says.

"And there's loads more coming. We've got Dune. We've got Doomsday," she says.

"I love film and TV. I think it's a really fun way to build community," she adds. "I'm just a fan. At the end of the day, I'm just a fan."

articles.title: Perez Hilton faces long recovery after reports he self-harmed during livestream
articles.text:
The US blogger Perez Hilton is in a "serious but stable" condition after being admitted to hospital, according to his family.

Emergency services were called to his Miami home on Tuesday after members of the public reported concerns while watching a TikTok livestream.

The Miami sheriff's office confirmed they attended a scene of a man "livestreaming acts of self-harm" on Tuesday. They did not confirm his name but said the man was alone in the house at the time.

A statement released on the 48-year-old's website said he "experienced significant blood loss" and his treatment and recovery would be a "long process".

The statement, external said Hilton was being held in hospital under Florida's Baker Act, which focuses on providing services for people experiencing a mental health crisis.

The father-of-three, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, is expected to have surgery in the coming days.

A TikTok spokesman said its automated moderation systems flagged the livestream to the company's US moderation team for review within minutes.

A moderator error caused a delay in the removal, TikTok said, but the company alerted law enforcement to the situation, closed several subsequent streams within 90 seconds, and banned the account.

The pseudonym Perez Hilton is a reference to Paris Hilton, who was at the height of her fame when the celebrity gossip blog was launched in 2005.

The website would go on to attract eight million hits a day at a time when the internet was still in its relative infancy. It was criticised for vicious commentary of stars including Miley Cyrus and Lady Gaga.

In later years, Hilton admitted having regrets about being "mean or cruel".

He has also appeared on reality TV shows including Celebrity Rap Superstar and Celebrity Big Brother.

articles.title: Madonna pays tribute to 'genius, otherworldly' producer William Orbit
articles.text:
Madonna has paid tribute to her regular collaborator and acclaimed music producer William Orbit, who died last month at the age of 69.

"You pressed a magic button inside of me and I fell into a galaxy of unrealised dreams," the pop superstar wrote on Instagram on Saturday. "Your music gave me a magic carpet to fly on and I visited many places."

Orbit's family announced "with profound sadness" on Friday that the Grammy-winning producer died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

The British producer, whose real name was William Wainwright, helped reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with Ray of Light, an album that blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

With its genre-bending sound, Ray of Light went on to win three Grammy Awards and is still considered by many to be the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

"I had an epiphany when I met you and started working with you," Madonna wrote in her post, alongside a video of herself standing beside Orbit to accept a Grammy Award. It also includes clips of the music videos and work she and Orbit created together.

Madonna said Orbit inspired her to sing and write in ways she never had before, without caring if her words "made sense or not".

"In many ways you were my Ray of Light - as was my daughter Lola who was born around this time," the singer wrote.
